## Start with a complete analysis

Routbreak describes the stochastic early phase of an epidemic in connected
communities. The reproduction matrix uses **destination rows and source
columns**: `R[i, j]` is the expected number of infections in community `i`
caused by one infected individual in community `j`.

The following hypothetical three-community system is supercritical and
strongly connected. Copy the complete block into a fresh R session after
installing the package.

```{r first-analysis}
library(Routbreak)

community <- c("North", "Central", "Coast")
R <- matrix(
  c(
    0.95, 0.12, 0.05,
    0.35, 0.85, 0.12,
    0.12, 0.25, 1.05
  ),
  nrow = 3,
  byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(destination = community, source = community)
)

risk <- rob_table(R)
risk
```

Each row of `risk` answers a question about an introduction into the named
source community:

- `outbreak_probability` is the probability that the branching process does
  not become extinct;
- `R_ob` compares expected offspring conditional on epidemic emergence with
  expected offspring conditional on extinction;
- `R_local` is the diagonal entry of `R`, counting infections that remain in
  the source community;
- `R_total` is the full source-column sum, counting infections generated in
  every destination; and
- `R_ref` is the spectral radius of the complete system and therefore has the
  same value in every row.

The three introduction locations have positive but unequal outbreak
probabilities. `R_local` alone does not rank their epidemic risk because it
ignores where exported infections go. `R_ob` is also not a community-specific
replacement for `R_ref`: it describes survival-conditioned offspring for a
particular introduction location, whereas `R_ref` characterizes growth of the
whole coupled system.

```{r first-probability-plot, fig.height=2.8, fig.cap="Outbreak probability for an introduction into each community in the hypothetical example."}
local({
  old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit(par(old_par), add = TRUE)
  x <- seq_len(nrow(risk))
  par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1.2, 0.8))
  plot(
    x, risk$outbreak_probability,
    type = "o", pch = 16, lwd = 2, col = "#0072B2", xaxt = "n",
    ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Introduction community",
    ylab = "Outbreak probability"
  )
  axis(1, at = x, labels = risk$community)
  text(
    x, risk$outbreak_probability,
    labels = sprintf("%.3f", risk$outbreak_probability),
    pos = 3, cex = 0.82, col = "#0072B2"
  )
})
```

## Installation

Routbreak is not yet available from CRAN. Install it from the public GitHub
repository with:

```{r install-github, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("peasantxuan/Routbreak")
```

The [package website](https://peasantxuan.github.io/Routbreak/) provides the
current function reference and tutorials.

## The four reproduction quantities

The individual functions behind `rob_table()` are useful when only one
quantity is needed.

```{r individual-functions}
r_ref(R)    # system-level reference reproduction ratio
r_local(R)  # infections that remain within each source community
r_total(R)  # infections generated anywhere by each source community
p <- outbreak_prob(R)
r_ob(R, p)  # supplied p is checked against the maximal fixed point
```

For Poisson offspring, outbreak probabilities satisfy

$$
p_i = 1 - \exp\left(-\sum_j R_{ji}p_j\right).
$$

Here $p_i$ refers to an introduction in source community $i$. The matrix is
transposed in the fixed point because `R[j, i]` describes infections generated
by source `i` in destination `j`.

For positive $p_i$, the Poisson outbreak reproduction ratio is

$$
R_i^{ob}=\frac{-\log(1-p_i)}{p_i}
          =\frac{\sum_jR_{ji}p_j}{p_i}.
$$

Consequently, $R_i^{ob}>1$ whenever $p_i>0$. Whether `R_ob` exceeds one is
therefore not, by itself, evidence that a community benefits from network
connections. Compare its magnitude and spatial variation across introduction
locations and with `R_local`, `R_total`, and the common `R_ref`.

## Change overall transmissibility

`scale_to_rref()` changes the system-level reproduction ratio without changing
the relative entries of the matrix.

```{r transmissibility, fig.cap="Outbreak probability and outbreak reproduction ratio as the same spatial matrix is scaled to different reference reproduction ratios."}
targets <- c(0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0)
scaled_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(targets, function(target) {
  scaled <- scale_to_rref(R, target)
  transform(rob_table(scaled), target_R_ref = target)
}))

colors <- c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73")
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1.5, 0.8))
plot(
  NA, xlim = range(targets),
  ylim = c(0, max(scaled_results$outbreak_probability)),
  xlab = expression(R[ref]), ylab = "Outbreak probability"
)
for (name in community) {
  selected <- scaled_results$community == name
  lines(
    scaled_results$target_R_ref[selected],
    scaled_results$outbreak_probability[selected],
    type = "o", col = colors[match(name, community)]
  )
}

plot(
  NA, xlim = range(targets), ylim = range(scaled_results$R_ob),
  xlab = expression(R[ref]), ylab = expression(R[ob])
)
for (name in community) {
  selected <- scaled_results$community == name
  lines(
    scaled_results$target_R_ref[selected], scaled_results$R_ob[selected],
    type = "o", col = colors[match(name, community)]
  )
}
legend("topleft", community, col = colors, lty = 1, pch = 1, bty = "n")
par(old_par)
```

Below threshold, an irreducible primitive Poisson matrix has zero outbreak
probability and the published continuation sets every `R_ob` to `R_ref`.
Above threshold, introduction locations can separate because their routes into
the surviving process differ.

## Import a long-format matrix

`as_rmatrix()` makes orientation explicit when reproduction means are stored
as directed edges.

```{r long-format}
edges <- expand.grid(
  destination = community,
  source = community,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
edges$mean_offspring <- mapply(
  function(destination, source) R[destination, source],
  edges$destination,
  edges$source
)

R_from_long <- as_rmatrix(
  edges,
  source = "source",
  destination = "destination",
  value = "mean_offspring",
  communities = community
)
identical(R_from_long, R)
```

By default, every directed pair must be present. An explicit row with value
zero creates a zero entry; an absent row is treated as unobserved and causes an
error. Set `missing = "zero"` only when the scientific data definition makes
absence equivalent to zero.

## Check matrix structure

```{r diagnostics}
is_irreducible(R)
matrix_diagnostics(R)
```

The component diagnostic identifies reducible matrices and reports each
strongly connected component's cyclic period. A period of one is primitive.
Periodicity matters for the generation-limit continuation below threshold;
Routbreak does not replace a non-existent limit for an imprimitive matrix with
an arbitrary cycle average.

## Assumptions and supported cases

The calculation is an early-epidemic, multitype branching-process
approximation with a fixed nonnegative reproduction matrix. Extinction means
that the transmission chain eventually ends. Outbreak probability is not the
final attack rate and does not describe epidemic size after emergence.

Poisson `r_ob()` supports supercritical irreducible systems, primitive
irreducible systems at or below threshold through the published continuation,
and diagonal matrices as independent communities. General reducible
non-diagonal matrices and periodic continuation cases are reported rather
than assigned an invented value. The advanced
[overdispersion tutorial](negative-binomial.html) covers independent-edge
negative-binomial offspring; the [inference tutorial](estimating-rob.html)
covers estimation from directed transmission data.

## Scientific reference

The definitions and continuation are from Wang B and Valdano E (2026),
“Redefining and estimating the early-phase reproduction ratio for epidemic
outbreaks in spatially structured populations,” *PLOS Computational Biology*
22(7): e1014425. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014425>
